claim: Human visual cortex is organized into multiple retinotopic maps.
source: Human visual cortex is organized into multiple retinotopic maps.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience, supported by extensive prior research and cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Characterizing the arrangement of retinotopic maps on the cortical surface is essential to many visual neuroscience studies.
source: Characterizing the arrangement of these maps on the cortical surface is essential to many visual neuroscience studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the introduction's discussion of various applications and citations to prior work.

claim: Traditional retinotopic maps are typically obtained by voxel-wise analysis of fMRI data.
source: Typically, maps are obtained by voxel-wise analysis of fMRI data.
evidence: This describes the standard method in the field, as established by prior literature.

claim: Traditional voxel-wise methods map only a portion of the visual field.
source: This method, while useful, maps only a portion of the visual field and is limited by measurement noise and subjective assessment of boundaries.
evidence: This is a known limitation of traditional methods discussed in the introduction.

claim: Traditional voxel-wise methods are limited by measurement noise.
source: This method, while useful, maps only a portion of the visual field and is limited by measurement noise and subjective assessment of boundaries.
evidence: This is a known limitation discussed in the context of traditional methods.

claim: Traditional voxel-wise methods are limited by subjective assessment of boundaries.
source: This method, while useful, maps only a portion of the visual field and is limited by measurement noise and subjective assessment of boundaries.
evidence: This limitation is discussed in the introduction and later in the manuscript.

claim: The novel Bayesian mapping approach combines a subject's retinotopic measurements from fMRI with a learned retinotopic atlas.
source: We developed a novel Bayesian mapping approach which combines observation–a subject's retinotopic measurements from small amounts of fMRI time–with a prior–a learned retinotopic atlas.
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution described in the abstract.

claim: The Bayesian process automatically draws areal boundaries.
source: This process automatically draws areal boundaries, corrects discontinuities in the measured maps, and predicts validation data more accurately than an atlas alone or independent datasets alone.
evidence: This is a stated capability of the method, demonstrated in the results.

claim: The Bayesian process corrects discontinuities in the measured maps.
source: This process automatically draws areal boundaries, corrects discontinuities in the measured maps, and predicts validation data more accurately than an atlas alone or independent datasets alone.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8B and discussed in the results.

claim: The Bayesian method predicts validation data more accurately than an atlas alone.
source: This process automatically draws areal boundaries, corrects discontinuities in the measured maps, and predicts validation data more accurately than an atlas alone or independent datasets alone.
evidence: This is demonstrated quantitatively in Figure 7 with cross-validation analysis.

claim: The Bayesian method predicts validation data more accurately than independent datasets alone.
source: This process automatically draws areal boundaries, corrects discontinuities in the measured maps, and predicts validation data more accurately than an atlas alone or independent datasets alone.
evidence: This is demonstrated quantitatively in Figure 7 with cross-validation analysis.

claim: Accurate measurement of retinotopic maps using fMRI is essential to a wide range of neuroscience and clinical applications.
source: Accurate measurement of these maps using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is essential to a wide range of neuroscience and clinical applications (Wandell and Winawer, 2011), in which they often provide a basis to compare measurements across individuals, groups, tasks, stimuli, and laboratories.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and general knowledge in the field.

claim: Retinotopic maps are employed to study homology between species.
source: In particular, maps are employed to study homology between species (Sereno and Tootell, 2005), cortical plasticity (Wandell and Smirnakis, 2009), individual variation in cortical function (Dougherty et al., 2003; Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011), and development (Van Essen, 1997; Conner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sereno and Tootell, 2005.

claim: Retinotopic maps are employed to study cortical plasticity.
source: In particular, maps are employed to study homology between species (Sereno and Tootell, 2005), cortical plasticity (Wandell and Smirnakis, 2009), individual variation in cortical function (Dougherty et al., 2003; Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011), and development (Van Essen, 1997; Conner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wandell and Smirnakis, 2009.

claim: Retinotopic maps are employed to study individual variation in cortical function.
source: In particular, maps are employed to study homology between species (Sereno and Tootell, 2005), cortical plasticity (Wandell and Smirnakis, 2009), individual variation in cortical function (Dougherty et al., 2003; Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011), and development (Van Essen, 1997; Conner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dougherty et al., 2003 and Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011.

claim: Retinotopic maps are employed to study development.
source: In particular, maps are employed to study homology between species (Sereno and Tootell, 2005), cortical plasticity (Wandell and Smirnakis, 2009), individual variation in cortical function (Dougherty et al., 2003; Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011), and development (Van Essen, 1997; Conner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Van Essen, 1997 and Conner et al., 2004.

claim: Many studies of cortical visual function in human include retinotopic mapping as a first step.
source: Many studies of cortical visual function in human, whether in motion (Huk et al., 2001), color (Engel et al., 1997a), object recognition (Grill-Spector et al., 1998), or attention (Martínez et al., 1999), include retinotopic mapping as a first step.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in different domains of visual function.

claim: The cortical magnification function can be used to understand visual performance.
source: Finally, basic properties of the maps themselves, such as the cortical magnification function (mm of cortex per degree of visual field), can be used to understand visual performance (Duncan and Boynton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duncan and Boynton, 2003.

claim: No method currently exists to fit a retinotopic map to a subject's cortical surface based on measurement without human intervention.
source: Despite their broad importance to neuroscience research, no method currently exists to fit a retinotopic map to a subject's cortical surface based on measurement, without human intervention.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Most retinotopic analyses of fMRI data use a voxel-wise approach.
source: Rather, most retinotopic analyses of fMRI data use a voxel-wise approach.
evidence: This describes the standard practice in the field.

claim: The general voxel-wise method involves measuring responses to mapping stimuli, deriving retinotopic coordinates for each voxel, and identifying areal boundaries by visual inspection.
source: The general method is (1) to measure responses to mapping stimuli, (2) to derive retinotopic coordinates for each voxel or surface vertex by analyzing traveling waves (Sereno et al., 1995; Engel et al., 1997b) or by solving a population receptive field (pRF) model (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008) for each voxel, and (3) to identify areal boundaries by visual inspection.
evidence: This describes the standard workflow with citations to key methods.

claim: Voxel-wise retinotopic mapping requires significant time and effort.
source: Aside from requiring significant time and effort, the maps that result from this process retain many common sources of error including distortion of the BOLD signal due to partial voluming (Dukart and Bertolino, 2014), vessel artifacts (Winawer et al., 2010), other sources of physiological noise, and model fitting biases (Binda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a known limitation of the traditional approach.

claim: Voxel-wise retinotopic maps retain many common sources of error including distortion of the BOLD signal due to partial voluming.
source: Aside from requiring significant time and effort, the maps that result from this process retain many common sources of error including distortion of the BOLD signal due to partial voluming (Dukart and Bertolino, 2014), vessel artifacts (Winawer et al., 2010), other sources of physiological noise, and model fitting biases (Binda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dukart and Bertolino, 2014.

claim: Voxel-wise retinotopic maps retain vessel artifacts.
source: Aside from requiring significant time and effort, the maps that result from this process retain many common sources of error including distortion of the BOLD signal due to partial voluming (Dukart and Bertolino, 2014), vessel artifacts (Winawer et al., 2010), other sources of physiological noise, and model fitting biases (Binda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winawer et al., 2010.

claim: Voxel-wise retinotopic maps retain model fitting biases.
source: Aside from requiring significant time and effort, the maps that result from this process retain many common sources of error including distortion of the BOLD signal due to partial voluming (Dukart and Bertolino, 2014), vessel artifacts (Winawer et al., 2010), other sources of physiological noise, and model fitting biases (Binda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Binda et al., 2013.

claim: Measured retinotopic maps have discontinuities.
source: Due to the various sources of noise, the measured maps have discontinuities and often systematically miss portions of the visual field, such as the vertical meridian (Silver et al., 2005; Larsson and Heeger, 2006; Swisher et al., 2007; Arcaro et al., 2009; Mackey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work documenting this issue.

claim: Measured retinotopic maps often systematically miss portions of the visual field, such as the vertical meridian.
source: Due to the various sources of noise, the measured maps have discontinuities and often systematically miss portions of the visual field, such as the vertical meridian (Silver et al., 2005; Larsson and Heeger, 2006; Swisher et al., 2007; Arcaro et al., 2009; Mackey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Measured retinotopic maps are limited by the available stimulus field of view in the scanner, often as little as 6–12° of eccentricity.
source: Further, the measured maps are limited by the available stimulus field of view in the scanner, often as little as 6–12° of eccentricity, and have difficulty measuring the foveal representation (Schira et al., 2009), the portion of the maps most important for many visual tasks including reading and object recognition (Malach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a known practical limitation of fMRI retinotopic mapping.

claim: Measured retinotopic maps have difficulty measuring the foveal representation.
source: Further, the measured maps are limited by the available stimulus field of view in the scanner, often as little as 6–12° of eccentricity, and have difficulty measuring the foveal representation (Schira et al., 2009), the portion of the maps most important for many visual tasks including reading and object recognition (Malach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schira et al., 2009.

claim: The foveal representation is the portion of the maps most important for many visual tasks including reading and object recognition.
source: Further, the measured maps are limited by the available stimulus field of view in the scanner, often as little as 6–12° of eccentricity, and have difficulty measuring the foveal representation (Schira et al., 2009), the portion of the maps most important for many visual tasks including reading and object recognition (Malach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malach et al., 2002.

claim: The shortcomings of traditional retinotopic mapping derive from the fact that it is organized around optimizing the explanatory power of retinotopy solutions from individual voxels.
source: These many shortcomings of the traditional retinotopic mapping process derive from the fact that it is organized around optimizing the explanatory power of the retinotopy solutions from individual voxels, rather than that of the entire visual field or cortical area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why traditional methods have limitations.

claim: Traditional voxel-wise methods yield maps that are neither smooth nor complete.
source: As a consequence, it yields maps that are neither smooth nor complete—nor grounded in any context of how the visual field is warped onto the cortical surface.
evidence: This is a characterization of the output of traditional methods.

claim: Traditional voxel-wise methods yield maps that are not grounded in any context of how the visual field is warped onto the cortical surface.
source: As a consequence, it yields maps that are neither smooth nor complete—nor grounded in any context of how the visual field is warped onto the cortical surface.
evidence: This is a characterization of the limitation of traditional methods.

claim: Lacking complete and smooth maps, the comparison of maps between subjects is difficult.
source: Lacking these data, the comparison of maps between subjects is difficult, and precise quantitative examination of individual differences is impossible.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the limitations described.

claim: Lacking complete and smooth maps, precise quantitative examination of individual differences is impossible.
source: Lacking these data, the comparison of maps between subjects is difficult, and precise quantitative examination of individual differences is impossible.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the limitations described.

claim: An alternative to voxel-wise modeling of fMRI data is to build a retinotopic atlas.
source: An alternative to voxel-wise modeling of fMRI data is to build a retinotopic atlas—a computational model of the mapping between visual field position and cortical structure.
evidence: This describes an alternative approach discussed in the introduction.

claim: Atlases are typically fit to a group-average description of function on the cortical surface after inter-subject cortical surface co-registration.
source: Atlases are typically fit to a group-average description of function on the cortical surface after inter-subject cortical surface co-registration (Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 1999a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dale et al., 1999 and Fischl et al., 1999a.

claim: The retinotopic prior is based on the Human Connectome Project group-average retinotopic maps.
source: The retinotopic prior is based on the Human Connectome Project (HCP) group-average retinotopic maps (Benson et al., 2018), shown here on an orthographic projection of the V1-V3 region.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Co-registration of surface anatomies between subjects improves the inter-subject alignment of cortical function.
source: Such descriptions are useful despite large inter-subject variation because co-registration of the surface anatomies between subjects improves the inter-subject alignment of cortical function as well.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The surface area of V1 can vary by 2- to 3-fold across healthy adults.
source: For example, the surface area of V1 can vary by 2- to 3-fold across healthy adults (Dougherty et al., 2003; Stensaas et al., 1974; Andrews et al., 1997), yet atlases of the mean anatomical locations (Wang et al., 2015) and the mean functional organization (Benson et al., 2012; Benson et al., 2014) of V1 can predict the functional organization of left-out subjects with high accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dougherty et al., 2003; Stensaas et al., 1974; and Andrews et al., 1997.

claim: Atlases of the mean anatomical locations and mean functional organization of V1 can predict the functional organization of left-out subjects with high accuracy.
source: For example, the surface area of V1 can vary by 2- to 3-fold across healthy adults (Dougherty et al., 2003; Stensaas et al., 1974; Andrews et al., 1997), yet atlases of the mean anatomical locations (Wang et al., 2015) and the mean functional organization (Benson et al., 2012; Benson et al., 2014) of V1 can predict the functional organization of left-out subjects with high accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015; Benson et al., 2012; and Benson et al., 2014.

claim: Atlases solve two problems of voxel-wise retinotopic maps: they represent the entire visual field and are smooth.
source: These atlases solve two of the problems of voxel-wise retinotopic maps: they represent the entire visual field and are smooth, but they are limited by the quality of the anatomical alignment and provide only a description of the mean—they cannot capture the idiosyncrasies of the maps in an individual subject because they assume that once a correspondence is found between the sulcal pattern in two subjects' visual cortices, the function will match.
evidence: This is a characterization of the advantages and limitations of atlases.

claim: Atlases are limited by the quality of the anatomical alignment.
source: These atlases solve two of the problems of voxel-wise retinotopic maps: they represent the entire visual field and are smooth, but they are limited by the quality of the anatomical alignment and provide only a description of the mean—they cannot capture the idiosyncrasies of the maps in an individual subject because they assume that once a correspondence is found between the sulcal pattern in two subjects' visual cortices, the function will match.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of atlas-based approaches.

claim: Atlases provide only a description of the mean and cannot capture the idiosyncrasies of the maps in an individual subject.
source: These atlases solve two of the problems of voxel-wise retinotopic maps: they represent the entire visual field and are smooth, but they are limited by the quality of the anatomical alignment and provide only a description of the mean—they cannot capture the idiosyncrasies of the maps in an individual subject because they assume that once a correspondence is found between the sulcal pattern in two subjects' visual cortices, the function will match.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of atlas-based approaches.

claim: A Bayesian model of retinotopic maps, combining data with a prior, will eliminate many issues with retinotopic mapping by optimizing the description of cortical retinotopic maps in the context of the full visual field and the corresponding cortex.
source: We hypothesize that a Bayesian model of retinotopic maps, combining data (retinotopic voxel- or vertex-wise measurements) with a prior (a full-field atlas derived from the anatomy), will eliminate many of the issues with retinotopic mapping described above by optimizing the description of cortical retinotopic maps in the context of the full visual field and the corresponding cortex (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the paper.

claim: Bayesian methods can describe cortical retinotopic maps in individual subjects more accurately than an atlas alone or measurements alone.
source: We propose that such methods can describe cortical retinotopic maps in individual subjects more accurately than an atlas alone or measurements alone.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis that is tested in the results.

claim: Previous work employing functional data to supplement global anatomical alignments between subjects has found an increase in the overlap of functional ROIs drawn from independent localizers.
source: First, previous work employing functional data to supplement global anatomical alignments between subjects has found an increase in the overlap of functional ROIs drawn from independent localizers (Frost and Goebel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Frost and Goebel, 2013.

claim: Even when subjects are aligned anatomically, appreciable and systematic differences in the structure-function relationship remain.
source: Thus, even when subjects are aligned anatomically, appreciable and systematic differences in the structure-function relationship remain.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited work and is a motivation for the current study.

claim: The basic form of the atlas (the prior) is sufficiently accurate that incorporating it will result in a more accurate estimate of the retinotopic map than the measurements alone.
source: Secondly, we believe that the basic form of the atlas (the prior) is sufficiently accurate that incorporating it will result in a more accurate estimate of the retinotopic map than the measurements alone.
evidence: This is a stated belief that motivates the Bayesian approach.

claim: The method employs a Bayesian maximum-likelihood optimization that describes the retinotopic maps in striate and extra striate cortex with previously infeasible precision.
source: The method we employ is a Bayesian maximum-likelihood optimization that describes the retinotopic maps in striate and extra striate cortex with previously infeasible precision.
evidence: This is a description of the method and its claimed advantage.

claim: The optimization builds on previous work using iterative approaches to fit and interpolate smooth retinotopic maps in individual subjects by incorporating an explicit prior and adopting an explicitly Bayesian formulation.
source: This optimization builds on previous work using iterative approaches to fit and interpolate smooth retinotopic maps in individual subjects (Dougherty et al., 2003) by incorporating an explicit prior in the place of human intervention and adopting an explicitly Bayesian formulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dougherty et al., 2003 and describes how the current work extends prior methods.

claim: Retinotopic mapping experiments were performed on eight subjects using fMRI.
source: Retinotopic mapping experiments were performed on eight subjects using fMRI.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Twelve individual retinotopy scans were performed on each subject.
source: Twelve individual retinotopy scans were performed on each subject then combined into 21 'training' datasets and 1 'validation' dataset for cross-validation as well as one full dataset of all scans for detailed analysis (Supplementary file 1; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The scans were combined into 21 'training' datasets and 1 'validation' dataset for cross-validation.
source: Twelve individual retinotopy scans were performed on each subject then combined into 21 'training' datasets and 1 'validation' dataset for cross-validation as well as one full dataset of all scans for detailed analysis (Supplementary file 1; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The prior map was derived from fitting a template to a high-quality dataset derived from 181 subjects in the Human Connectome Project.
source: The prior map (Figure 2B), used for methods 2 and 3, was derived from fitting a template to a high-quality dataset derived from 181 subjects in the Human Connectome Project (Uğurbil et al., 2013; Van Essen et al., 2013; Benson et al., 2018) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the HCP and describes the source of the prior.

claim: The inferred retinotopic maps provide high-quality descriptions of the full retinotopic topology for each subject's V1-V3 regions.
source: The inferred retinotopic maps, predicted by Bayesian inference, provide high-quality descriptions of the full retinotopic topology for each subject's V1-V3 regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the results.

claim: Inferred maps can be produced even in the absence of observed retinotopic measurements (i.e., using the prior alone).
source: These maps can be produced even in the absence of observed retinotopic measurements (i.e., using the prior alone), or by combination with retinotopic data.
evidence: This describes a capability of the method.

claim: The inferred maps have all the advantages of the retinotopic prior while also accounting for idiosyncrasies in individual maps.
source: In this latter case, the inferred maps have all the advantages of the retinotopic prior (topologically smooth maps, predictions beyond the stimulus aperture, etc.), while also accounting for idiosyncrasies in individual maps.
evidence: This is a summary of the advantages of the Bayesian approach.

claim: In constructing the Bayesian-inferred retinotopic map for a single hemisphere, two deformations are performed: anatomical registration and retinotopic registration.
source: In constructing the Bayesian-inferred retinotopic map for a single hemisphere, we perform two deformations, detailed in Figure 4 (see also Materials and methods): (1) we first deform that hemisphere's inflated surface to register it to an average anatomical atlas using FreeSurfer (leftmost arrow in Figure 4C); and (2) we then further deform the surface to register it to the retinotopic prior, based on the hemisphere's retinotopic measurements (second arrow in Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the two-step process of the method.

claim: The first deformation accounts for structural differences across subjects.
source: In step 1, we account for structural differences across subjects—the deformation that occurs for this registration is unique for each subject.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the first deformation represents.

claim: The second deformation accounts for the differences in the relationship between structure and function across subjects.
source: In step 2, we account for the differences in the relationship between structure and function across subjects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the second deformation represents.

claim: The deformations applied in the last step indicate meaningful individual differences in the structure-function relationship.
source: Although it is possible that deformations in step two partly compensate for imperfections in the first two registrations, we propose that, to a first approximation, the deformations applied in the last step indicate meaningful individual differences in the structure-function relationship.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the second deformation.

claim: There are some subjects for whom there are large differences between the retinotopic atlas defined by the prior and the atlas defined by the Bayesian fit.
source: There are some subjects for whom there are large differences between the retinotopic atlas defined by the prior and the atlas defined by the Bayesian fit (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Where there are discrepancies between the prior and Bayesian map, the Bayesian inferred map is more accurate.
source: Where there are discrepancies, the Bayesian inferred map is more accurate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison to validation data in Figure 5B.

claim: For some subjects, the prior alone is a good fit to the retinotopic data.
source: For some other subjects, the two atlases are in closer agreement such that the prior alone is a good fit to the retinotopic data (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5C.

claim: The mean deformation distance across vertices is 3.3° ± 0.6° for the anatomical alignment.
source: Overall, the mean deformation distance across vertices is 3.3° ± 0.6° (µ ± σ across subjects) of the cortical sphere for the anatomical alignment and 3.4° ± 0.4° for the retinotopic alignment.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The mean deformation distance across vertices is 3.4° ± 0.4° for the retinotopic alignment.
source: Overall, the mean deformation distance across vertices is 3.3° ± 0.6° (µ ± σ across subjects) of the cortical sphere for the anatomical alignment and 3.4° ± 0.4° for the retinotopic alignment.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The mean angle between the anatomical and retinotopic deformations is 83.0° ± 9.6°.
source: The mean angle between these deformations is 83.0° ± 9.6° (note that this last measurement is in terms of degrees of rotational angle rather than degrees of the cortical sphere).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The alignment of the V1-V3 region to the retinotopic prior increases the standard deviation of the surface curvature across subjects.
source: The alignment of the V1-V3 region to the retinotopic prior increases the standard deviation of the surface curvature across subjects, suggesting that retinotopic alignment is not simply an improvement on FreeSurfer's curvature-based alignment.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Retinotopic alignment is not simply an improvement on FreeSurfer's curvature-based alignment.
source: The alignment of the V1-V3 region to the retinotopic prior increases the standard deviation of the surface curvature across subjects, suggesting that retinotopic alignment is not simply an improvement on FreeSurfer's curvature-based alignment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that curvature variability increases after retinotopic alignment.

claim: The retinotopic alignment is sacrificing some amount of structural uniformity across subjects in order to accommodate the individual differences in subjects' structure-to-function mapping.
source: This suggests that the retinotopic alignment is sacrificing some amount of structural uniformity across subjects in order to accommodate the individual differences in subjects' structure-to-function mapping, and is consistent with our interpretation that there are substantial individual differences in the mapping between retinotopy and surface topology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the curvature variability results.

claim: There are substantial individual differences in the mapping between retinotopy and surface topology.
source: This suggests that the retinotopic alignment is sacrificing some amount of structural uniformity across subjects in order to accommodate the individual differences in subjects' structure-to-function mapping, and is consistent with our interpretation that there are substantial individual differences in the mapping between retinotopy and surface topology.
evidence: This is supported by the deformation analysis and curvature variability results.

claim: The large individual differences that remain, even after structural co-registration, point to the importance of using at least some individual subject functional data when inferring the maps.
source: The large individual differences that remain, even after structural co-registration (Figure 6C), point to the importance of using at least some individual subject functional data when inferring the maps, rather than assuming the atlas (prior) is correct.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the variability observed in Figure 6C.

claim: The maps predicted via Bayesian inference were highly accurate irrespective of the amount of data used to inform the fits.
source: The maps predicted via Bayesian inference were highly accurate irrespective of the amount of data used to inform the fits (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated quantitatively in Figure 7.

claim: Between inferred maps informed by 3.2 min and 19.2 min of scan time, the scaled MSE of the prediction remains in the range of ~0.4–0.5.
source: Between those inferred maps informed by 3.2 min of scan time (one scan) and 19.2 min (six scans), the scaled MSE of the prediction remains in the range of ~0.4–0.5.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation analysis.

claim: When the range is limited to 3 to 12 deg, the MSE is much lower, ~0.20–0.26.
source: These scaled errors are larger near the fovea because the denominator used for scaling the error metric (i.e., the eccentricity) could be very small; when the range is limited to 3 to 12 deg, the MSE is much lower,~0.20–0.26.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The mean absolute polar angle error from a Bayesian map derived from a single 3.2 min scan is 25° ± 11°.
source: Expressed separately in units of polar angle and eccentricity, the mean absolute polar angle error from a Bayesian map derived from a single 3.2 min scan is 25° ± 11° and the mean absolute eccentricity error is 0.76° ± 0.34° (µ ± σ across 96 datasets).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The mean absolute eccentricity error from a Bayesian map derived from a single 3.2 min scan is 0.76° ± 0.34°.
source: Expressed separately in units of polar angle and eccentricity, the mean absolute polar angle error from a Bayesian map derived from a single 3.2 min scan is 25° ± 11° and the mean absolute eccentricity error is 0.76° ± 0.34° (µ ± σ across 96 datasets).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: For the prior alone, the polar angle error is 34° ± 12° and the eccentricity error is 1.3° ± 0.17°.
source: For the prior alone, these errors are substantially higher: 34° ± 12° for polar angle and 1.3° ± 0.17° for eccentricity.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The accuracy of the predictions from data alone was highly influenced by scan time.
source: In contrast to the inferred maps for which the accuracy is largely independent of scan time, the accuracy of the predictions from data alone was highly influenced by scan time.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: The scaled MSE of the maps predicted from the training datasets alone ranged from ~2.2 (3.2 minutes of training data) to ~0.3 (19.2 minutes of training data).
source: The scaled MSE of the maps predicted from the training datasets alone for the same range of scan times ranged from ~2.2 (3.2 minutes of training data) to ~0.3 (19.2 minutes of training data).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation analysis.

claim: With more than ~11 min of scan time, the predictions made from the training datasets alone have a slightly lower scaled MSE than those made from Bayesian inference.
source: With more than ~11 min of scan time, the predictions made from the training datasets alone have a slightly lower scaled MSE than those made from Bayesian inference; although, notably, the improvements in scaled MSE for more than 11 min of scan time are small.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Predictions derived from the anatomically-defined atlas alone are more accurate than predictions from 3.2 min of scanning.
source: Predictions derived from the anatomically-defined atlas alone are more accurate than predictions from 3.2 min of scanning and only slightly less accurate than predictions from training datasets derived from 6.4 min of scanning; this is in agreement with previous analyses of prediction error versus measurement error in retinotopic mapping experiments (Benson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The predictions using the prior alone were universally less accurate than the Bayesian predictions.
source: The predictions using the prior alone were universally less accurate than the Bayesian predictions (Figure 7, cyan)—for all subjects and all training datasets, the combination of prior with data improved prediction accuracy compared to the anatomical prior alone.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: For all subjects and all training datasets, the combination of prior with data improved prediction accuracy compared to the anatomical prior alone.
source: The predictions using the prior alone were universally less accurate than the Bayesian predictions (Figure 7, cyan)—for all subjects and all training datasets, the combination of prior with data improved prediction accuracy compared to the anatomical prior alone.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation analysis.

source: Subjects performed a task in which they were required to attend to the fixation dot and indicate when its color changed.

source: Spatial distortions due to inhomogeneities in the magnetic field were corrected using in-house software from NYU's Center for Brain Imaging (http://cbi.nyu.edu/software).

claim: The data were motion-corrected by co-registering all volumes of all scans to the first volume of the first scan in the session.
source: The data were then motion-corrected by co-registering all volumes of all scans to the first volume of the first scan in the session.
evidence: This is a description of the preprocessing step.

claim: The fMRI slices were co-registered to the whole brain T1-weighted anatomy, and the time series resampled via trilinear interpolation to the 1 mm3 voxels within the cortical ribbon (gray matter).
source: The fMRI slices were co-registered to the whole brain T1-weighted anatomy, and the time series resampled via trilinear interpolation to the 1 mm3 voxels within the cortical ribbon (gray matter).
evidence: This is a description of the preprocessing step.

claim: The time series were averaged for each voxel across all scans with the same stimulus within a given dataset.
source: Finally, the time series were averaged for each voxel across all scans with the same stimulus within a given dataset.
evidence: This is a description of the preprocessing step.

claim: Retinotopic maps were produced by solving linear, circularly symmetric population receptive field (pRF) models for each voxel using Vistasoft.
source: Retinotopic maps were produced by solving linear, circularly symmetric population receptive field (pRF) models for each voxel using Vistasoft, as described previously (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008.

claim: pRF models were solved using a two-stage coarse-to-fine approach on the time series in the 1 mm3 gray matter voxels.
source: pRF models were solved using a two-stage coarse-to-fine approach on the time series in the 1 mm3 gray matter voxels.
evidence: This is a description of the pRF modeling procedure.

claim: The first stage of the model fit was a grid fit, solved on time series that were temporally decimated (2×), spatially blurred on the cortical surface using a discrete heat kernel, and subsampled by a factor of 2.
source: The first stage of the model fit was a grid fit, solved on time series that were temporally decimated (2×), spatially blurred on the cortical surface using a discrete heat kernel (approximately equal to a Gaussian kernel of 5 mm width at half height), and subsampled by a factor of 2.
evidence: This is a description of the pRF modeling procedure.

claim: The parameters obtained from the grid fit were interpolated to all gray matter voxels and used as seeds for the subsequent nonlinear optimization.
source: The parameters obtained from the grid fit were interpolated to all gray matter voxels and used as seeds for the subsequent nonlinear optimization.
evidence: This is a description of the pRF modeling procedure.

claim: The pRF parameters were projected from the volume to the cortical surface vertices for white, mid-gray, and pial surfaces using nearest-neighbor interpolation.
source: Finally, the pRF parameters were projected from the volume to the cortical surface vertices for white, mid-gray, and pial surfaces using nearest-neighbor interpolation; values were then averaged across the three layers using a weighted-mean in which the fraction of BOLD signal variance explained by the pRF model was used as a weight.
evidence: This is a description of the pRF projection procedure.

claim: All vertices with a pRF variance explained fraction less than 0.1 were ignored.
source: All vertices with a pRF variance explained fraction less than 0.1 were ignored.
evidence: This is a description of the thresholding applied.

claim: To generate initial models of the retinotopic maps, boundaries for 12 retinotopic maps were hand-drawn.
source: To generate our initial models of the retinotopic maps, we begin by hand-drawing boundaries for 12 retinotopic maps.
evidence: This is a description of the model generation procedure.

claim: These boundaries need only be drawn once for a single group-average retinotopic map.
source: These boundaries need only be drawn once for a single group-average retinotopic map.
evidence: This is a description of the model generation procedure.

claim: The boundaries are projected onto the cortical surface, and the retinotopic coordinates for each vertex on the surface are deduced via a minimization procedure.
source: The boundaries are projected onto the cortical surface, and the retinotopic coordinates for each vertex on the surface are deduced via a minimization procedure.
evidence: This is a description of the model generation procedure.

claim: The minimization routine simultaneously maximizes both the smoothness of the retinotopic fields between vertices connected by edges in the mesh as well as the overall orthogonality between the polar angle field and the eccentricity field.
source: To this end, the minimization routine simultaneously maximizes both the smoothness of the retinotopic fields between vertices connected by edges in the mesh as well as the overall orthogonality between the polar angle field and the eccentricity field.
evidence: This is a description of the minimization objective.

claim: Group-average retinotopic maps were obtained from 181 subjects whose data were published and made freely available as part of the Human Connectome Project.
source: Group-average retinotopic maps (Supplementary file 2B) were obtained from 181 subjects whose data were published and made freely available as part of the Human Connectome Project (Benson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benson et al., 2018.

claim: The cortical surfaces of the fsaverage left and right hemispheres were inflated both to a smooth hemisphere and to a sphere.
source: The cortical surfaces of the fsaverage left and right hemispheres, on which the group-average data were constructed, were inflated both to a smooth hemisphere (FreeSurfer's 'inflated' surface) as well as to a sphere (FreeSurfer's 'sphere' surface); the vertices on the spherical surfaces were then flattened to 2D maps using an orthographic map projection.
evidence: This is a description of the cortical surface processing.

claim: The initial vertex coordinates of the map projections were warped in order to bring the polar angle and eccentricity measurements of the vertices into alignment with the 2D model's predictions of retinotopy while maintaining topological constraints.
source: The initial vertex coordinates of the map projections described above were warped in order to bring the polar angle and eccentricity measurements of the vertices into alignment with the 2D model's predictions of retinotopy while maintaining topological constraints: that is preventing triangles in the triangle mesh representing the 2D cortical map from inverting and penalizing excessive stretching or compression of the map.
evidence: This is a description of the registration procedure.

claim: The potential function F is a sum of two kinds of penalties: penalties for deviations from the reference mesh and penalties for mismatches between the vertices with retinotopic coordinates and their positions in the retinotopic model.
source: Fundamentally, the potential function F is a sum of two kinds of penalties: penalties for deviations from the reference mesh and penalties for mismatches between the vertices with retinotopic coordinates and their positions in the retinotopic model.
evidence: This is a description of the potential function.

claim: The potential function was minimized using a gradient descent algorithm sensitive to the singularities in the terms Ge and Gθ.
source: The potential function was minimized using a gradient descent algorithm sensitive to the singularities in the terms Ge, and Gθ (Table 2); whenever the singularity is accidentally crossed, the minimizer backtracks and chooses a smaller step-size.
evidence: This is a description of the minimization algorithm.

claim: This approach prevents the inversion of any triangle in the mesh.
source: This approach prevents the inversion (from counter-clockwise ordering to clockwise ordering) of any triangle in the mesh, as such an inversion would require the minimization trajectory to pass through a singularity at the point where α = 0 or α = π.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the algorithm preserves topology.

claim: Minimization was run for at least 2500 steps in which the step-size was constrained such that the displacement of each vertex in each step was at most 1/50th of the average edge-length in the map projection.
source: Minimization was run for at least 2500 steps in which the step-size was constrained such that the displacement of each vertex in each step was at most 1/50th of the average edge-length in the map projection.
evidence: This is a description of the minimization parameters.

claim: A small amount of exponentially distributed random noise was added to the gradient at each step with the constraint that the gradient direction at each vertex be conserved.
source: A small amount of exponentially distributed random noise was added to the gradient at each step with the constraint that the gradient direction at each vertex be conserved; this noise did not affect the minimum obtained by the search but did speedup convergence significantly (see associated libraries for further details).
evidence: This is a description of a technique used to speed up convergence.

claim: Convergence was generally observed within 1000–2000 steps.
source: Convergence was generally observed within 1000–2000 steps.
evidence: This is an observation about the convergence behavior.

claim: The registered vertex coordinates give the alignment of the subject's cortical surface to the model of retinotopy.
source: The registered vertex coordinates, once obtained, give the alignment of the subject's cortical surface to the model of retinotopy; accordingly, a prediction of any vertex's associated pRF and visual area label can be derived by comparing the the vertex's registered coordinates with the model.
evidence: This is a description of how predictions are made from the registration.

claim: Because only the vertex coordinates, and not the vertex identities, are changed during the registration process, there is no need to invert the registration.
source: Because only the vertex coordinates, and not the vertex identities, are changed during the registration process, there is no need to invert the registration: visual area label, polar angle, and eccentricity values assigned to each vertex apply as readily to the vertices whether they are visualized in the registered vertex coordinates or in the coordinates that define the subject's white-matter surface, for example.
evidence: This is an explanation of a property of the registration method.

claim: The predicted map from the group-averaged data provides a reasonable estimate of any subject's expected retinotopic map.
source: Because the group-average retinotopic data were used in the registration, the predicted map that results provides a reasonable estimate of any subject's expected retinotopic map, as shown previously (Benson et al., 2012; Benson et al., 2014); although the predicted map does not account for further individual differences in the structure to function relationship, as we show in this paper.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A retinotopic map prediction for any new subject can be easily obtained by using FreeSurfer to align the new subject's cortical surface with the fsaverage subject's surface then to project the retinotopic maps from the fsaverage subject to the new subject based on the anatomical similarity between them.
source: Additionally, because the predicted map from the group-averaged data is defined on the fsaverage subject's cortical surfaces, a retinotopic map prediction for any new subject, for whom retinotopic mapping measurements may not be available, can be easily obtained: one can use FreeSurfer to align the new subject's cortical surface with the fsaverage subject's surface (anatomical structure alignment) then to project the retinotopic maps from the fsaverage subject to the new subject based on the anatomical similarity between them.
evidence: This is a description of how the atlas can be applied to new subjects.

claim: The atlas is similar but not identical to one presented previously.
source: The atlas is similar but not identical to one presented previously (Benson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benson et al., 2014.

claim: For each subject, their cortical surface was aligned based on anatomical structure to the fsaverage subject's cortical surface using FreeSurfer.
source: For each subject, their cortical surface was aligned based on anatomical structure to the fsaverage subject's cortical surface using FreeSurfer, then their retinotopic data were projected to a map using the identical map projection described above in the section on the anatomically-defined atlas of retinotopy.
evidence: This is a description of the individual subject processing.

claim: The individual subject's projected map is then arranged according to the registered vertex coordinates from the anatomically-defined atlas of retinotopy.
source: The individual subject's projected map is then arranged according to the registered vertex coordinates from the anatomically-defined atlas of retinotopy; this step reflects the prior belief that the group-average registration to the retinotopy model is generally accurate for an individual subject when that subject's anatomical structure has been aligned to the fsaverage subject's.
evidence: This is a description of how the prior is applied to individual subjects.

claim: If no retinotopic measurements are made for a subject, then the prediction of retinotopy for that subject would be identical to the prediction of retinotopy contained in the anatomically-defined atlas.
source: If, for a subject, no retinotopic measurements are made, then there is no data with which to modify this prior belief; accordingly, the prediction of retinotopy for that subject would be identical to the prediction of retinotopy contained in the anatomically-defined atlas.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the Bayesian framework.

claim: The next step registers the individually measured retinotopy data to the anatomically-defined atlas.
source: The next step registers the individually measured retinotopy data to the anatomically-defined atlas.
evidence: This is a description of the Bayesian inference step.

claim: The mesh is resampled to the same uniform triangle mesh used as the initial vertex coordinates in the registration of the anatomically-defined atlas of retinotopy in order to speedup registration.
source: The mesh is resampled to the same uniform triangle mesh used as the initial vertex coordinates in the registration of the anatomically-defined atlas of retinotopy in order to speedup registration.
evidence: This is a description of a technique used to improve computational efficiency.

claim: For each training dataset of each subject, minimization was run for 2500 steps using the same protocol that was used with the anatomically-defined atlas of retinotopy.
source: For each training dataset of each subject, minimization was run for 2500 steps using the same protocol that was used with the anatomically-defined atlas of retinotopy.
evidence: This is a description of the minimization procedure for individual subjects.

claim: Cortical magnification was calculated using both the observed retinotopic maps and the inferred maps that were produced by combining each subject's full retinotopy dataset with the retinotopic prior.
source: Cortical magnification was calculated using both the observed retinotopic maps and the inferred maps that were produced by combining each subject's full retinotopy dataset with the retinotopic prior.
evidence: This is a description of the cortical magnification analysis.

claim: Cortical magnification was calculated by first projecting all vertices in a single visual area into the visual field based on their pRF centers.
source: Cortical magnification was calculated by first projecting all vertices in a single visual area (such as V1) into the visual field based on their pRF centers.
evidence: This is a description of the cortical magnification calculation method.

claim: The cortical magnification of a particular polar angle and eccentricity is the total white vertex surface-area of all pRF centers within a disk of some radius α, divided by the area of the disk.
source: The cortical magnification of a particular polar angle and eccentricity is then the total white vertex surface-area (as calculated by FreeSurfer) of all pRF centers within a disk of some radius α, divided by the area of the disk (πα2).
evidence: This is a description of the cortical magnification calculation method.

claim: For an eccentricity ρ, a radius α = ρ/3 was used.
source: For an eccentricity ρ, we used a radius α = ρ/3.
evidence: This is a description of a parameter used in the cortical magnification calculation.
